title: Idolatry Made Sense: The Gods of Israel's Neighbors
subtitle: Idols were not stupidity. They were a sophisticated technology of presence and control, and the pull they answered has not gone anywhere.

sections.title: They Were Not Fools
sections.body:
The Old Testament's long war against idolatry can look, to a modern reader, like a war against stupidity. Who bows to a statue he carved himself. We read the prophets, shake our heads at the ancients, and move on, quietly congratulating ourselves for worshiping nothing so visible.

That reading fails in two directions at once. It makes ancient people fools, which they were not. And it makes idolatry a museum piece, which it is not.

No thoughtful Babylonian believed his god simply was the statue and nothing more. The image was something stranger and more plausible than that. Until we understand what an idol actually was, we cannot understand why Israel kept sliding toward them for eight hundred years, or why the prophets fought them with everything they had. I want to understand it, because the hunger the idols answered is the hunger I carry into every anxious week.

sections.title: Washing the Mouth of a God
sections.body:
In Mesopotamia, a newly carved image was not yet a god. It had to be activated. Craftsmen finished the statue, and then priests performed a ritual called mis pi, the washing of the mouth, together with a rite of opening the mouth. Egypt had its own opening of the mouth ceremony. Through these rites the image was understood to become a living interface, a body the deity could inhabit and act through, seeing, breathing, eating. In the ritual the craftsmen even disclaimed their own work, swearing in effect that the gods, not their hands, had made the image.

After activation, the image was treated as a person of the highest rank. Priests woke it in the morning, washed it, dressed it, set meals before it daily, and carried it through the streets at festivals. The god was fed, clothed, housed, and entertained by the city it protected.

So an idol was manufactured presence. A god you could locate, visit, and serve, and who therefore needed you. The theology was sophisticated, and nearly the whole ancient world held some version of it. Israel was commanded to live next door to all of this with no image of their own God at all. An empty throne above the ark. Nothing about that was easy.

sections.title: Baal Was Agricultural Insurance
sections.body:
In Canaan the dominant rival was Baal, the storm god. We know him well now. In 1929, excavations at Ras Shamra on the Syrian coast uncovered the ancient city of Ugarit and its tablets, including the Baal cycle, a sequence of myths written in a language close to biblical Hebrew. Baal rides the clouds. He battles the sea. He falls to Death and rises again, and his return brings the rains that raise the grain.

Understand what that meant to a farmer. Egypt drinks from the Nile, but Canaan, as Deuteronomy puts it, drinketh water of the rain of heaven. No rain meant no harvest, and no harvest meant watching your children weaken. Baal claimed to be the one who opened the sky, and his cult promised that the right rituals at the right times would keep it open.

So Baal worship was not exotic. It was agricultural insurance. It was the religion of making sure. Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel was not a seminar on comparative religion. It was a public test, held in the third year of a drought, of who actually sends rain.

sections.title: A God You Can Manage
sections.body:
This is why idolatry made sense, and why it seduced Israel for centuries. An idol is a god you can manage. You know where he lives. You know what he eats. You feed him and clothe him, and the relationship runs on a logic any farmer understands. Service in, blessing out. The whole system promised what every anxious heart wants, which is control over outcomes through technique.

The God of Israel refused the entire arrangement. No image, so he cannot be located and handled. No feeding, for if I were hungry, I would not tell thee, he says in Psalm 50, for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof. He binds himself in covenant, but he will not be operated. He will be trusted, or he will be left.

And trust is exactly what we would rather not give. A managed god asks for ritual at the appointed hours. A living God asks for everything, on no schedule we control. Given the choice, Israel kept choosing the god who could be managed. So do I.

sections.title: The Satire That Refuses the Theology
sections.body:
Now the prophetic polemic comes into focus. Isaiah 44 follows a carpenter through his day. He cuts down a cedar, burns part of it to bake his bread and warm himself, and from the residue carves a god and bows down to it. Psalm 115 runs the same blade. They have mouths, but they speak not. Eyes have they, but they see not. They that make them are like unto them.

The prophets surely knew about the mouth-washing rituals and the elaborate theology of presence. The satire ignores all of it on purpose. That refusal is the point. Strip away the ceremony, the prophets insist, and what remains is a man worshiping his own manufacture, asking a block of wood to give what only the Maker of wood can give. Whatever the priests claimed the ritual accomplished, the prophets called the thing what it was.

We did not outgrow this. We still make things and then ask the things to save us. The portfolio, the platform, the body, the brand, the candidate. They have mouths and speak not, and the old warning still holds. We become like what we worship. The prophets are not finished with their audience.
